title: this week's portion
hookLine: this week's portion; the mountain ahead is a calendar
carry: join the cycle wherever it is

lines: THE SAME CHAPTERS, THE SAME WEEK.
cards: This Saturday morning, in a synagogue in Buenos Aires, one in Melbourne, one in a Brooklyn basement and one in a Jerusalem neighborhood, the scroll will be opened, most weeks, to the same place.
The same chapters, read in the same week, in the same order, by people who will never meet. Some people could tell you this week's portion by name without checking. It's a calendar made of text.
And as camp one ends, it's also the road ahead of you on this path. Today: the portion, and where it's about to take us.

teach.b: A parsha is a portion. The five books of the Torah are divided into fifty-four of them, and one is read each Sabbath, so the whole scroll is read in about a year.
There are fewer Sabbaths than portions in some years, so some weeks two are read together.

teach.h: EACH NAMED FOR AN EARLY WORD.
teach.b: Each portion is named for one of its first distinctive words. The first is Bereshit, in the beginning. Then Noach, Noah.
Then Lech Lecha, go forth, when Abraham leaves home. Some people date things by it, the way others use the month: that happened the week of Noach. The reading isn't only on Saturday morning.

Short pieces are read on Monday and Thursday mornings too. The rabbis traced that custom back to the time of Moses, so that no one would go three days without Torah, and credited the scribe Ezra with shaping it.
They even suggested a way to study it at home: read the week's portion twice, and once in translation. And here's a detail that says a lot about a scattered people.
After some holidays, Israel and the rest of the world fall out of step by a week, and then quietly catch up again.
The cycle bends, but it holds. That's why the carry for today is what it is. You don't start the Torah on page one when you're ready.
You find out where everyone is, and you step in there. Camp one gave you twenty-one words. Next, camp two: the stories, and it begins exactly where the cycle does, at the first word, Bereshit.

how: Jews read the weekly Torah portion aloud from the scroll in synagogue on Sabbath mornings, with shorter readings on Monday and Thursday mornings and Sabbath afternoons, and many study it at home during the week.

practice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell, to walk back through camp one. Let the words come one by one: the mezuzah, the candles, mensch, seder, the glass, mitzvah, machloket. Abraham, Jacob, Sinai, Shabbat, shalom, the Shema, kavanah.
Bracha, tzedakah, minyan, Yom Kippur, teshuvah, Torah, the parsha. Stay with whichever one pulls at you.

wordCard.voice: The parsha. This week's portion, one of fifty-four, read by a whole people in step. Twenty-first word. Camp one, complete.
